items.title: Kidney biopsy: gold standard
items.contentHtml:
Diagnosis requires kidney biopsy

  • The kidney biopsy is the gold standard; clinical suspicion (nephrotic syndrome, non-diabetic proteinuria) is not enough to confirm amyloidosis.
  • In renal biopsy, the amyloid deposit is located in the mesangium, glomerular basement membrane, interstitium and vessels; vascular involvement can be isolated.
  • The sample must include renal cortex with ≥8 glomeruli to evaluate glomerular pattern and avoid false negatives due to sampling.
  • Examination trap: renal biopsy can be normal in the initial phases if the deposit is exclusively vascular or interstitial; repeat if suspicion is high.
  • Routine hematoxylin-eosin staining shows acellular eosinophilic material, but confirmation with Congo red and polarization microscopy is required.

items.foco: Congo red stain with green birefringence
items.title: Congo red and birefringence
items.contentHtml:
Congo red stain with green birefringence

  • The Congo red stain is the classic histochemical test; amyloid stains orange-red.
  • Confirmation requires apple-green birefringence when observing with polarized light; This phenomenon is pathognomonic.
  • False positives for Congo red occur in dense collagen fibers or elastin; green birefringence helps differentiate.
  • False negatives: very thin samples, discoloration or inadequate fixation; use known positive controls.
  • Electron microscopy shows unbranched fibrils 7-12 nm in diameter; useful when staining is doubtful.

items.foco: Amyloid A is associated with chronic inflammation
items.title: Amyloid A (AA) and causes
items.contentHtml:
Amyloid A is associated with chronic inflammation

  • AA amyloidosis (amyloid A protein) is derived from the serum precursor serum amyloid A protein, an acute phase reactant produced by the liver.
  • It is associated with chronic inflammation: rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, familial Mediterranean fever, tuberculosis, bronchiectasis or inflammatory bowel disease.
  • Familial Mediterranean fever is the most common hereditary cause of AA amyloidosis; treatment with colchicine (dose 1-2 mg/day) prevents deposits.
  • AA amyloidosis typically affects the kidney, spleen, liver and adrenal gland; cardiac involvement is rare, unlike AL.
  • Differential diagnosis: in AA amyloidosis immunohistochemistry is positive for amyloid A, while in AL it is negative.

items.foco: Amyloid AL by monoclonal light chains
items.title: AL amyloid and dyscrasia
items.contentHtml:
AL amyloid due to monoclonal light chains

  • AL amyloidosis (amyloid light chain) is produced by the deposition of fragments of monoclonal light chains of immunoglobulins, generally lambda (λ) in ~75% of cases.
  • The underlying cause is a plasma cell dyscrasia: multiple myeloma (10-15%) or Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS).
  • AL amyloidosis is the most common form of systemic amyloidosis in developed countries; It affects kidney, heart, liver, peripheral nerves and soft tissues.
  • Detection of monoclonal protein in serum or urine is performed with electrophoresis and immunofixation; serum kappa/lambda ratio (free light chain assay) is useful.
  • renal biopsy with light chain staining (immunohistochemistry or immunofluorescence) confirms type; the absence of staining for amyloid A supports AL.

items.foco: Nephrotic syndrome is the most common presentation
items.title: Nephrotic syndrome
items.contentHtml:
Nephrotic syndrome is the most common presentation

  • The most common renal presentation of amyloidosis is nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria >3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminemia <3 g/dL, edema, hyperlipidemia).
  • Proteinuria is usually massive, non-selective, and can reach nephrotic ranges at the time of diagnosis.
  • Microhematuria and hypertension can coexist, but are not predominant; Its presence does not rule out amyloidosis.
  • Nephrotic syndrome in an elderly patient with monoclonal gammopathy should raise the suspicion of AL amyloidosis rather than membranous glomerulonephritis.
  • Kidney function may be preserved at the beginning; Progression to end-stage renal failure is variable, more rapid in AL without treatment.

items.title: Other urinary findings
items.contentHtml:
Microhematuria and hypertension can coexist

  • Microhematuria (dysmorphocytes or not) is observed in 20-30% of patients with renal amyloidosis; It is not an exclusion criterion.
  • Hypertension is present in ~30-50% of cases, less frequent than in other glomerulopathies; It may appear due to vascular deposition.
  • The coexistence of microhematuria and hypertension does not differentiate amyloidosis from other causes of nephrotic syndrome; biopsy is mandatory.
  • Proteinuria may be selective in early stages, but becomes non-selective with progression.
  • Trap: in AA amyloidosis hypertension is less common than in AL; orthostatic hypotension suggests autonomic or adrenal involvement.

items.title: Kidney ultrasound
items.contentHtml:
Enlarged kidneys on ultrasound

  • Enlarged kidneys on ultrasound is a characteristic finding in early stages, with hyperechogenic parenchyma due to amyloid infiltration.
  • Unlike advanced chronic kidney disease (small kidneys), in amyloidosis the kidneys can be normal or large even with renal failure.
  • Ultrasound is not diagnostic; It is only a guide, since other infiltrative diseases (lymphoma, leukemia) can also increase kidney size.
  • In late stages, the kidneys can decrease in size due to fibrosis, but they rarely reach the degree of atrophy of other nephropathies.
  • Measuring kidney size is useful for planning percutaneous renal biopsy and ruling out contraindications (small kidneys or cysts).

items.foco: Deposit in mesangium and glomerular basement membrane
items.title: Glomerular histological pattern
items.contentHtml:
Deposition in the mesangium and glomerular basement membrane

  • The deposition in the mesangium and glomerular basement membrane is the typical pattern; nodular mesangial expansion may mimic diabetic glomerulosclerosis.
  • In light microscopy, amyloid is seen as acellular eosinophilic material that expands the mesangium and thickens the basement membrane.
  • Congo red stain is positive; green birefringence is seen in areas of deposition.
  • Immunofluorescence may show staining for light chains in AL (usually lambda) or amyloid A in AA; there are no immune complex deposits.
  • Electron microscopy reveals amyloid fibrils in the mesangium and along the basement membrane, with loss of podocytes.

items.foco: Monoclonal protein in serum or urine
items.title: Monoclonality detection
items.contentHtml:
Monoclonal protein in serum or urine

  • Monoclonal protein in serum or urine is detected by protein electrophoresis and immunofixation; the sensitivity of electrophoresis alone is low (~50% in AL).
  • Immunofixation in serum and urine increases the sensitivity to >90% to detect the paraprotein.
  • The serum free light chains assay (kappa/lambda ratio) is essential; an abnormal relationship with elevation of one chain suggests monoclonality.
  • In AL amyloidosis, monoclonal protein may be scarce or absent on electrophoresis; immunofixation and free light chains are more sensitive.
  • The absence of monoclonal protein in serum or urine does not exclude AL amyloidosis; ~10% of cases have negative immunofixation, but abnormal free light chains.

items.foco: Treatment of AL with chemotherapy or transplant
items.title: Management of AL amyloidosis
items.contentHtml:
Treatment of AL with chemotherapy or transplant

  • The goal of treatment in AL amyloidosis is to eradicate the light chain-producing plasma cell clone.
  • The first line in eligible patients is chemotherapy with a regimen based on bortezomib, cyclophosphamide and dexamethasone (CyBorD) or Combined daratumumab.
  • Autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (bone marrow transplant) is reserved for patients with good functional status, without severe cardiac involvement and aged <65-70 years.
  • Response criteria include reduction of monoclonal protein and free light chains, improvement of proteinuria and stabilization of renal function.
  • The chemotherapy can cause kidney toxicity; adjust drug doses according to creatinine clearance and monitor tumor lysis syndrome.

items.foco: AA amyloidosis responds to underlying disease control
items.title: Management of AA amyloidosis
items.contentHtml:
AA amyloidosis responds to control of the underlying disease

  • The main treatment of AA amyloidosis is the aggressive control of the underlying inflammatory disease (arthritis, infection, autoimmune).
  • In familial Mediterranean fever, colchicine at doses of 1-2 mg/day reduces production of amyloid and prevents renal progression.
  • In other causes, use biological drugs (anti-TNF, anti-IL-6) or immunosuppressants depending on the etiology; The remission of inflammation stops the deposit.
  • Proteinuria can decrease or stabilize if the underlying disease is controlled; amyloid regression is possible but slow.
  • Measure acute phase reactants (C-reactive protein, serum amyloid A) to monitor inflammatory activity and adjust treatment.

items.foco: Dialysis or transplant in end-stage renal disease
items.title: Renal replacement therapy
items.contentHtml:
Dialysis or transplant in end-stage renal disease

  • end-stage renal disease (glomerular filtration rate <15 mL/min/1.73m2 or need for dialysis) requires renal replacement therapy.
  • dialysis (hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis) is an option; Hemodialysis may be associated with a greater risk of hypotension if there is autonomic involvement.
  • Kidney transplantation is viable in selected patients; in AL amyloidosis prior chemotherapy is required to achieve hematological response before transplantation.
  • In AA amyloidosis, kidney transplantation has good survival if the inflammatory disease is controlled; Recurrence in the graft is possible if inflammation persists.
  • Graft survival in amyloidosis is lower than in other causes, especially in AL with extra-renal involvement; evaluate heart and nervous system.
